articles.title: Live Updates: Obama, Harris to campaign for Democrats in 3 battleground states; Trump travels to Georgia
articles.summary: President Trump has held rallies throughout the week in Iowa, Kansas, Florida and more, but leaders of the Democratic Party are set to hold a midterm blitz of their own on Saturday ahead of Election Day. Former President Obama is expected to make two Midwest trips to Cleveland, Ohio and Detroit, Mich. to help move…
articles.body:
President Trump has held rallies throughout the week in Iowa, Kansas, Florida and more, but leaders of the Democratic Party are set to hold a midterm blitz of their own on Saturday ahead of Election Day.

Former President Obama is expected to make two Midwest trips to Cleveland, Ohio and Detroit, Mich. to help move the needle for Democrats in the two battleground states.

Obama will first travel to Ohio to hold a rally with former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), who is locked in a tight battle with Ohio Republican Jon Husted for the Buckeye State’s Senate seat.

According to The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), Brown has a 51 percent chance to defeat Husted and is anticipated to be one of the tightest races in this year’s midterms.

Following Obama’s Cleveland rally, he will travel north to Detroit to campaign with Michigan’s Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who is facing former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.).

DDHQ has El-Sayed holding a steady lead over Rogers, 68 percent to 32 percent, respectively.

Former Vice President Harris will also be hitting the campaign trail on Saturday, meeting up with Democratic Senate candidate Chris Pappas (N.H.) in Portsmouth, N.H.

Pappas is facing off against Republican challenger John Sununu for the chance to succeed Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.).

Despite the Democrat frenzy, Trump is not done with his midterm tour. The president will hold a 7 p.m. rally in Perry Ga. in an attempt to boost Republican Senate candidate Rep. Mike Collins, who is going up against incumbent Democrat Sen. Jon Ossoff.

The president will also rally in Port Huron, Mich., Corinth, Miss. and Lubbock and Waco, Texas next week.

articles.title: DOJ demands California counties identify noncitizen voters: Reports
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Friday sent letters to election officials in every California county asking that they identify potential noncitizens on their voter rolls, according to several reports. The letter warned local officials would “risk significant federal scrutiny” if they failed to comply with this request, The New York Times reported, citing a…
articles.body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Friday sent letters to election officials in every California county asking that they identify potential noncitizens on their voter rolls, according to several reports .

The letter warned local officials would “risk significant federal scrutiny” if they failed to comply with this request, The New York Times reported, citing a spokesperson for the U.S. attorney’s office in Los Angeles.

The DOJ’s letters included a list of people federal officials claimed the agency has identified as possible noncitizens who may receive ballots through California’s practice of sending a ballot to every registered voter in the state.

The DOJ gave local officials 48 hours “to identify who on the accompanying list is a citizen and who is not.”

The top federal prosecutor in Southern California, Bill Essayli, said in a statement shared on social media that the request was “simple.”

“California does not verify citizenship status. We did the work for them,” he wrote. “We obtained the registered voter list and told them who we believe are noncitizens on their rolls.

articles.title: Trump hints that White House press area may be moved to another location
articles.summary: President Trump pushed back Saturday morning against reports he was considering replacing the White House press briefing room with an indoor swimming pool but said he was considering moving media “to a less obnoxious location.” On Tuesday, The New York Times reported Trump expressed to aides he would like to bring back an indoor pool…
articles.body:
President Trump pushed back Saturday morning against reports he was considering replacing the White House press briefing room with an indoor swimming pool but said he was considering moving media “to a less obnoxious location.”

On Tuesday, The New York Times reported Trump expressed to aides he would like to bring back an indoor pool installed in 1933 during the Franklin D. Roosevelt administration. The pool was later covered under former President Richard Nixon to make space for the briefing room.

“There is a Fake News report out there that I am going to remove the White House Press Room and bring back the old Swimming Pool, which lies directly underneath,” Trump wrote on Truth Social .

“Although I may move the Fake News to a less obnoxious location, the old swimming pool will never be brought back,” he continued. “I NEVER even thought to do such a stupid thing!”

The president and his administration have increasingly sought to restrict press access due to unfavorable reporting throughout his second term.

This week, the White House stripped The Independent’s Andrew Feinberg of his print press pool duties, barring him from traveling with the president after Trump lashed out at the reporter in the Oval Office.

White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA) President Jacqui Heinrich accused the White House of acting in “retaliation.”

“The American public’s right to an independent press depends on reporters being able to do their jobs without fear that challenging the president will cut off their access,” Heinrich said in a statement .

A White House spokesperson defended the move in a Wednesday evening statement to The Hill.

“No person and no journalist has a constitutional right to access the President’s Oval Office, Air Force One, or other sensitive and private facilities,” the spokesperson said. “When publications lie, fabricate, and ignore the truth, proximity matters less and they can write their fiction from outside of these secure facilities.”

Last month, the WHCA also condemned the Trump administration’s decision to bar Politico, CNN and MS NOW from the White House. The move drew widespread criticism and an order from a federal judge to reinstate the media credentials to journalists from these outlets. Though CNN reporters, like Feinberg, are still unable to join the press pool on Air Force One.

articles.title: ‘You have this superpower’ — how the left is weaponizing jury nullification
articles.summary: The effort is to engineer “Twelve Angry Men” scenarios on real juries — but unlike in the movie, the jurors are actually being trained to ignore evidence and deliberations in favor of political outcomes.
articles.body:
That statement from Qiana Johnson is part of reported training material for residents to engage in “jury nullification,” whereby jurors ignore the law and incriminating facts in a given case to nullify any prosecution.

Notably, Johnson is the newly elected clerk of Prince George’s County Circuit Court in the Maryland suburbs of Washington. She is part of a growing left-wing movement gaining traction with voters that calls for radical changes to the U.S. legal system.

The effort is to engineer “Twelve Angry Men” scenarios on real juries — but unlike in the movie, the jurors are actually being trained to ignore evidence and deliberations in favor of political outcomes.

In her election campaign for her current job, Johnson had to overcome questions about her own criminal record . But many voters are willing to give others a second chance when they show evidence of rehabilitation and contrition. The more immediate concern might be embracing a practice that is expressly barred by courts.

Johnson is part of a new investigation by the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee into groups training citizens to engage in jury nullification — including Free DC and Harriet’s Wildest Dreams, where Johnson was reportedly a board member.

One such document allegedly declares, “You have this superpower, and that superpower is you are able to nullify that goddamn jury.”

Far-left professors have long advocated that juries use jury nullification. Georgetown Law professor and MSNBC legal analyst Paul Butler has long advocated that Black jurors engage in nullification in cases involving Black defendants. Butler wrote in the Washington Post in 2016: “Confronting the racial crisis in criminal justice, jury nullification gives jurors a special power to send the message that Black lives matter.”

The problem of biased jurors has long plagued the legal system. It can work both ways in ignoring the law to refuse or secure convictions. Past cases involving President Trump and other Republicans have raised bias concerns over the jury pool in cities such as Washington, D.C., and New York City.

But jury nullification is different; it is a direct assault on the very foundation of the American court system. The juror is the thumping heart of that system — a group of empowered citizens who swear to consider cases without prejudice or prejudgment.

It is not a crime to advocate jury nullification. Moreover, there are legitimate concerns raised by investigations into such groups. about chilling the rights of free speech and association. In my view, such advocacy is protected speech under the First Amendment.

But that is not always the case for lawyers, who can face professional consequences. Many courts bar lawyers from arguing for jury nullification. Calling for jury nullification can also present sanctionable conduct for lawyers in a given case.

Even if this is protected speech, voices in both parties need to denounce these efforts. It effectively encourages jurors to lie when they take their oath to follow the law and to shed any outside bias or prejudgment. It is an effort to enlist jurors in using cases to achieve political and social goals at the expense of the rule of law.

The professors and pundits supporting these campaigns are actively seeking a hostile takeover of the courts without explaining to these citizens the implications of such dishonesty. Indeed, Comer has detailed how groups like Freedom Trainers are allegedly seeking to enlist potential jurors while, according to the committee, instructing trainees not to “signal the agenda.”

Instead of addressing the impact of politicizing our jurors, these groups are portraying nullification as “a powerful tool for ensuring fairness and justice.”

These efforts are coming at a time of full assault on our judicial system from the left. Leading Democrats are calling for the packing of the Supreme Court, to reverse decisions with which they disagree. Every leading Democratic candidate for the 2028 presidential nomination has now thrown the court to the baying mob.

Former Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton is only the most recent , declaring, “We should seriously look at expanding the court while the Democrats are in power.”

From the trial jury to the Supreme Court, many on the left now seek to take control of institutions that have long been the rock of this Republic. If successful, justice will become merely an extension of politics.

What is so disconcerting is that there is no longer any pretense of principle. Law professors are demanding that pledges to pack the Court be used as litmus tests for politicians, and senators are calling for an instant liberal majority on the Court to carry out the “will of the people.”

Liberal professors have long demanded revolutionary change to “ reclaim America from constitutionalism .”

The attack on the American jury may be the most insidious of these efforts. Our legal system invests average citizens with the power to do justice. Every community plays a role in upholding the principles of blind justice. As with court-packing, jury nullification is a previously odious practice now being portrayed as a noble cause. It is part of the conditioning of voters to accept foundational changes to our constitutional system, to further a radical agenda harmful to the nation.

The juror’s role was indeed a “superpower,” but not the one these professors and pundits are pushing. It was a power against prejudice and partisanship; it was the power of doing simple justice in a nation committed to the rule of law.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the New York Times best-selling author of “ Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution .”

articles.title: Omar’s deleted tweet could give clue on alleged brother marriage
articles.summary: A deleted 2013 Father's Day post by Ilhan Omar referred to her father as "Nur Said," a name similar to her ex-husband's, raising new questions.
articles.body:
A deleted 2013 social media post in which Rep. Ilhan Omar , D-Minn., appeared to refer to her father by a different name has resurfaced as federal investigators examine questions surrounding her identity and immigration records.

"Happy Father's Day to my aabo Nur Said, I am forever grateful to Allah for giving me the best father …," Omar wrote in the June 2013 post, which was deleted in 2019.

Several records, including a memorial post by the Congressional Black Caucus marking his death in 2020, refer to Omar's father as "Nur Omar Mohamed." But the now-deleted X post has Omar calling him "Nur Said," a name that also appears similar to the name of her former husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi.

The congresswoman deleted the social media post the morning of Sept. 19, 2019.

An archived version of the post, first reported on by the Daily Caller in 2019, resurfaced after federal agents searched Omar's Washington, D.C., residence on Oct. 12 as part of an ongoing criminal investigation into possible false statements on immigration and naturalization documents. Omar and her office have repeatedly denied allegations that her former husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, is her brother.

She has also denied wrongdoing amid the federal probe, which she has called a political attack.

Somali names generally consist of a person's given name, their father's given name and their paternal grandfather's given name. The similarity between names alone does not establish a familial relationship.

A statement allegedly attributed to Omar's spokesperson and recirculated online said "Nur Said" was her father's childhood nickname and that he maintained a public page using the name. The statement also said the tweet was deleted because Omar and her family had received threats.

Omar's office did not respond Friday to Fox News Digital's request for comment on the now-deleted social media post.

Omar's father is referred to as "Nur Said" in some reports. For example, a New York Post story on his alleged military experience quoted Oxford University historian Mohamed Haji Ingiriis as calling Omar's father "Nur Said."

Fox News has not independently verified that Omar's father's name is Nur Said Elmi Mohamed, his alleged name, not Nur Omar Mohamed.

In a statement to Fox News Digital on Thursday, a spokesperson for the congresswoman said Omar has "repeatedly and unequivocally denied" the "baseless, disgusting conspiracy theory" that she married her brother .

The spokesperson pointed to Omar's interview Wednesday on MS NOW, in which she was asked whether her one-time husband may have been a "distant relative."

Recent court documents related to the search warrant for Omar's Washington, D.C. residence, first obtained by Fox News Digital, connected to the federal investigation identify Omar as " Ilhan Nur Said Elmi , a.k.a. Ilhan Abdullahi Omar." The filing does not explain why the name appears in the document or establish that Omar used a false identity.

Omar told Fox News Digital on Friday that her "real name" is "Ilhan Abdullahi Omar" and not "Ilhan Nur Said Elmi."

"Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, you know it," Omar told Fox News Digital when asked about her name. "It's Ilhan Abdullahi Omar."

Omar's marriage to Elmi ended in divorce in 2017. She later legally married Ahmed Hirsi in 2018.

Two people familiar with the investigation told Fox News Digital that "Ilhan Nur Said Elmi" may be Omar's legal name. Omar's office has disputed that characterization.

A former Minnesota federal immigration judge told Fox News Digital that if investigators prove Omar knowingly used a false name on federal forms, the conduct could be brought into question under the federal false-statements statute , 18 U.S.C. § 1001. Whether the statute applies would depend on the specific documents, the materiality of any alleged misstatement and the evidence of intent.

The Justice Department did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Hannah Brennan contributed to this report.

articles.title: A GOP congressman in a swing district faces angry voters: ‘I’m against the party that caused this’
articles.summary: GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick was weaving through the crowd of a fall street festival when he was confronted by a man enraged by the skyrocketing costs he’s exp...
articles.body:
GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick was weaving through the crowd of a fall street festival when he was confronted by a man enraged by the skyrocketing costs he's experiencing.

Dave Woods, a contractor and registered Democrat, held up red signs with big white letters in Fitzpatrick's face to show how his heating oil and diesel fuel costs have shot up in the last year. But Fitzpatrick walked away to head to his speech.

"Where's Mr. Fitzpatrick to get in the photo shot here?" Woods told CNN after the exchange. "I'm against the party that caused this."

Farther down the street, Ted Wassmer, a registered Republican who has supported the congressman in the past, was weighing his vote in the November election. Wassmer's woodworking business has been hit hard by the Trump administration's tariffs and rising inflation. A combat veteran who has never supported President Donald Trump, Wassmer called the Iran war an "absolute joke."

"It's a clown show in DC right now," Wassmer said. "I may vote against Republicans having dominance of the Congress, that may be my decision to get the administration in check. And I'm not very happy with Democrats either. I kind of think the left and the right are running rampant right now, so I have to kind of really look at it."

Fitzpatrick is one of the only Republicans in Congress fighting for reelection in a district Kamala Harris won in 2024 — and Democrats see this as their best chance in a decade to win the seat.

Following the congressman on a recent day of campaigning offered an inside look at how the vulnerable Republican is trying to hold onto his battleground district in the suburbs of Philadelphia despite a toxic political environment for his party. Woods was not the only frustrated voter to come up to the congressman with complaints. But Fitzpatrick believes he can keep his seat by distancing himself from his own party and attempting to find common ground.

"If they're angry at Pete Hegseth, take it out on Pete Hegseth. If they're angry at Donald Trump or Joe Biden or Kamala Harris, take it out on them at the ballot box, but don't take it out on people that are not them that have never espoused their views," Fitzpatrick told CNN in a wide-ranging interview.

Describing himself as politically homeless in the two-party system, Fitzpatrick says he would register as an independent if Pennsylvania opens its primaries to independent voters and lowers the threshold for independent candidates to get on the ballot.

"I'm a registered Republican from when I was 18, but I did that because of Ronald Reagan. That party no longer exists," Fitzpatrick said.

But Democrats plan to use his party affiliation against him . Nationally, Democrats have become increasingly confident they will win the House, hoping that voter concerns over the status quo will lead to losses for Republicans. A new CNN poll found Trump's approval rating stands at a record low, and voters express broad dissatisfaction with the economy and the state of the country nearly two years into unified GOP control of the federal government.

Fitzpatrick's Democratic challenger, Bucks County Commissioner Bob Harvie, hopes to tap into voter frustration and reluctance to support the Republican ticket to flip the district and bring his party one step closer to reclaiming the House majority.

"He's changed. He's not the same guy he was when we sent him there. You know, he's a guy that was supposed to fight against corruption as a former FBI agent, and this is the most corrupt administration in American history. And he's not doing anything about it," Harvie told CNN. "He hasn't stood up for the people here, and plus we've got the mood of this country and the pain that people are feeling is different than anything that's happened before."

Fitzpatrick has withstood national headwinds before, including the blue wave of 2018 when Democrats flipped the House. Democrats believe, however, that his attempts to distance himself from his party now might not be enough to overcome the palpable anger of many of his constituents, and are investing millions in this race for the first time in six years as a result. Democrats have spent over $10 million in advertisements since September, according to AdImpact. Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro has also invested heavily in the race and has appeared with Harvie on the campaign trail.

Democrats knew going into the final stretch that Bucks County voters have a history of making their decisions late in the game, which is in part why national Democratic groups started ramping up their spending in the district in the final weeks, according to a Democratic strategist working on House races.

To defend against the influx of Democratic cash, the Republican fundraising apparatus has parachuted in, including $100,000 from super PAC MAGA Inc., according to Federal Election Commission filings, and $4.9 million from the Republican outside campaign arm earlier this month for advertisements. In a sign of how difficult the race has become, Fitzpatrick spent $5 million of his own war chest between July and September.

"They take their shots when the climate is such that they think that, you know, that it's a wise investment for them," Fitzpatrick said of Democrats. "So, they think."

The two candidates have not faced off directly to debate, even though both have made offers. Fitzpatrick, a former FBI agent, has claimed Harvie has been the subject of an FBI investigation, while Harvie says he never was and argues Fitzpatrick is trying to recycle old claims.

But all of the mudslinging on television and posturing online hasn't necessarily translated to real life. On Saturday, when the two candidates had a chance encounter as they both waited to speak at an event in Bristol, they ignored each other.

Four swing districts in Pennsylvania could be key to winning control of the House in November.

On paper, Fitzpatrick's seat should be the easiest for Democrats to flip given his left-leaning district, but the congressman's voting record and endorsement list make it difficult for Democrats to easily put him in a box, and Democrats privately concede this is their hardest race in the state, according to multiple Democratic operatives and sources.

Fitzpatrick was one of two House Republicans to vote against Trump's signature package of tax and federal spending cuts in July, dubbed the "big beautiful bill," even though he was a decisive vote for an earlier version of the legislation that passed the House in May. He has voted to rein in Trump's war with Iran, but only after it passed the 60-day clock on the use of military force without congressional authorization.

He recently signed on to a new effort to force a vote on releasing more of the Jeffrey Epstein files. He did not back an initial effort to force a vote to compel the Justice Department to release millions of pages of files, but he did vote in favor of that earlier Epstein files push when it came to the floor. And on multiple occasions, he has helped Democrats bring their legislation to the floor. Fitzpatrick has signed on to more discharge petitions — a maneuver to circumvent House GOP leadership to bring bills to the floor — than any other Republican this Congress.

He was early to sound the alarm that Republicans did not have a plan to address the affordability crisis, and he worked with Democrats in the House to try to extend the enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies that expired at the end of 2025. He is a fierce advocate for Ukraine and vowed to end Trump's unpopular $1.8 billion compensation fund that critics said would be used to pay out the president's allies. He's the only Republican running for federal office to receive an endorsement from the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of labor unions in the country. In 2024, Fitzpatrick voted for former UN Ambassador Nikki Haley for president, snubbing Trump.

Former Sen. Joe Manchin, who dropped his Democratic party affiliation to become an independent, told CNN that he endorsed Fitzpatrick because of their strong working relationship in Congress.

"I don't look at the party, I look at the person, and I got to be honest with you, Brian is just the right person to be serving. I don't even know the other gentleman. I'm sure he's an upstanding person. I never go out and campaign against anybody. I just know when you've got a good one, you ought to keep him," Manchin told CNN. "The Democrats will be able to work with Brian as well as they will anybody else if it's good for our country."

Harvie has looked to poke holes in Fitzpatrick's voting record and argued that his votes against his party either are inconsistent or don't change the outcome. He has questioned why Fitzpatrick is receiving money from the Republican Party if he claims to be an independent voice. And while Fitzpatrick meets with various groups throughout the district, Harvie has questioned why the congressman hasn't held a formal town hall in years.

"I don't really know the last time he's cast a vote that matters against the president," Harvie argued. "The president and (House Majority Leader) Mike Johnson have been putting millions of dollars into his campaign to boost him up because they're afraid he's going to lose. So, if he's really that independent, why doesn't he give that money back?"

'I'm upset': Undecided voters still weighing critical vote

Both candidates have their work cut out for them in the final two weeks before Election Day. Even with the onslaught of ads and campaign events, there are still voters in the district who say they haven't made up their minds.

But some of Fitzpatrick's supporters are having a particularly hard time given their broader frustrations with Trump and the Republican Party.

Retired Air Force member Nathaniel Gagum is a registered Republican who has voted for Fitzpatrick in the past but says he has been horrified by some of the administration's military actions and its treatment of veterans. Gagum, who referred to Trump as a "draft dodger," is furious that Trump fired Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. C.Q. Brown . He says the Iran war should never have happened, and he could not believe Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth outlined plans for a public livestream of a firing squad execution. (Trump later called off the plan for the livestream after public outcry.)

"I'm upset," Gagum, who said he is still undecided, told CNN. Referring to Fitzpatrick, he said , "I'm questioning a lot because of some of the things I see in Congress and how you vote with Congress, and how you side with Trump, and you side with things that goes against our interests, my interests, my veterans."

Becky Berg, a nurse and a registered Libertarian, has voted for Fitzpatrick in previous elections. But she told CNN her costs have gotten more expensive in the last two years, and she is worried about the rights of her LGBTQ+ friends and family who she says have been targeted by some of the Trump administration's policies.

"Honestly, I'm just thinking about getting Republicans out of office for the most part. I will, before I vote, I will look into the candidates and try and be as informed as I can be. But I am not a fan of Trump and a lot of the policies he has been pushing. So, I'm kind of just looking at changing the current regime," Berg told CNN.

In a potential warning sign for Democrats hoping for staying power beyond a potential wave this cycle, a number of Pennsylvania voters who said they were going to support Harvie said their support was more reactionary to the current environment than about Harvie himself.

"I think the biggest thing is it's less about pro-Bob Harvie and more anti-Fitzpatrick. I just don't think that he does everything that he's claimed that he's wanted to do, and I think it's time for somebody else to be given a shot," Julia Corrado, a social media manager, told CNN of her intended vote for Harvie.

If Fitzpatrick is able to overcome the environment, it will be because of voters like Joe, a 70-year-old retired EPA worker, who went up to Fitzpatrick on Saturday to shake his hand and share that he can separate his frustration with Trump (whom he called a "slime ball") from the congressman.

"I'm a realist. I look at each individual," he said.

Some Pennsylvanians have felt so let down by their leaders that they have given up on the electoral process and plan either not to vote or to write in their own candidate.

Jason Green, a restaurant owner of 20 years, sat in his empty cheesesteak shop in Langhorne during what should have been the middle of a weekend dinnertime rush.

"It's at the point where it's almost not worth being in business," Green said.

Green, a registered independent, voted for Trump in 2024 after initially supporting Robert F. Kennedy Jr. He told CNN he challenged both Fitzpatrick and Harvie to donate the money they were raising for their campaigns to the local community, but said both declined. He plans to write in a different name on the ballot as a result.

"I've checked out," Green said. "They're both idiots in my eyes. Simple as that. I'm done."

About an hour away on the opposite side of the district, John Barchard, 43, was resolved in his decision to not participate in the midterm election.

Barchard, who works in marketing, has never been registered with either party and has voted for both Democrats and Republicans. He voted for Harris in 2024; in 2020, he supported former Joe Biden; and he's supported Fitzpatrick in the past. But now, his frustration with both parties has reached a boiling point because he says neither has done enough to address the needs of the working class. He views Republicans as having capitulated to Trump and criticizes Democrats for not fighting hard enough.

"It's not a 'what's the point?' It's, 'I don't want blood on my hands anymore' because every time we vote one way, it doesn't balance out the other, in my opinion. And there needs to be more options," Barchard told CNN. "The system is not working for anybody."

But somehow, Barchard says he still has hope.

"For some dumb reason, as a millennial, I still love this country and I still think it works. I think the experiment is great and it's taken a wrong turn," he said.

articles.title: José Andrés joins fight against proposed DC foie gras ban
articles.summary: World renowned chef José Andrés is entering the battle over Washington’s proposed ban on foie gras, a delicacy which animal rights activists have called cruel. Andrés responded to a proponent of the ban, labeled as Initiative 86 on D.C.’s ballot, in a post to the social platform X — appearing to argue serving the French…
articles.body:
World renowned chef José Andrés is entering the battle over Washington’s proposed ban on foie gras, a delicacy which animal rights activists have called cruel.

Andrés responded to a proponent of the ban, labeled as Initiative 86 on D.C.’s ballot, in a post to the social platform X — appearing to argue serving the French specialty made with fattened duck liver is no different ethically than making other meat-based dishes.

“ L et’s ban beef and pork and chicken … and also vegetables too because is [sic] a study that says that maybe indications of suffering,” Andrés wrote. “We have children hungry in USA and the World … lets end hunger and then we talk.”

Foie gras is a delicacy made from duck liver which is enlarged via force feeding before slaughter. Washington animal rights activists are pushing for the ban over concerns about cruelty, putting them at odds with the city’s restaurant industry.

Andrés owns restaurants all over the world a nd has long been an advocate for addressing world hunger. He founded the World Central Kitchen, a nonprofit which aims to provide meals to those impacted by natural disasters.

But Andrés is not the only restaurant owner pledging to fight the ban. Bart Hutchins, owner of Butterworth’s in D.C., authored an op-ed in The Washington Post defending the use of foie gras and the practice by which it is made.

“Ducks are not humans,” Bart wrote. “This overfeeding is something the bird does naturally. Before their annual migration, ducks gorge — they stuff themselves with excess food … What foie gras farming does is amplify a natural biological process rather than invent a cruel one.”

Hutchins announced on X that Butterworth’s will be having a “Foie Gras at the End of the World” event with a four-course tasting menu, available every day Oct. 27 through Election Day.

The Butterworth’s owner told Axios D.C. he would continue to serve foie gras even if it is banned, and if the ballot initiative passes, he would rather move his restaurant to Virginia than stop offering the delicacy to its patrons.

articles.title: How to navigate AI manipulation this election season
articles.summary: The challenge for voters is learning how to question suspicious content without assuming everything they encounter is fake.
articles.body:
An attacker doesn’t have to change a single vote to damage confidence in an election. Sometimes, creating confusion is enough. We can protect the systems that run elections and still leave voters exposed to manipulation.

For example, in 2024 , Iranian cyber actors stole private campaign material and attempted to distribute it to influence the election. U.S. intelligence agencies also attributed a fabricated video showing ballots being destroyed in Pennsylvania to Russian actors. These different tactics shared the goal of exploiting division and undermining confidence.

Artificial intelligence makes that challenge more complicated. It can make deception cheaper, faster and easier to personalize, but the risk goes beyond creating more convincing fakes. It can also make it easier for dishonest actors to cast doubt on real evidence by claiming it was generated by AI.

Social engineering exploits how people think, whom they trust and what prompts them to act. During an election, attackers have plenty to work with, including strong emotions, familiar public figures and a constant stream of consequential information.

Consider a hypothetical call that sounds like a candidate asking for an urgent donation. Or a text claiming your polling location has changed. Or a video appearing to show an election official admitting misconduct. Each exploits a familiar identity or institution, and AI can help attackers produce convincing variations at scale.

The same approach can target campaign staff. An attacker impersonating a colleague could use a cloned voice to request an authentication code. One successful deception could expose private communications that are then leaked, selectively edited or used to support a misleading narrative.

An attack might begin with a social media post, continue with a fake website and conclude with a text. However, seeing a claim repeatedly does not make it independently verified.

The deeper problem emerges when awareness of deception turns into disbelief of everything. Legal scholars Bobby Chesney and Danielle Citron call this the “liar’s dividend.” As people become more aware of deepfakes, dishonest actors gain a more plausible excuse to dismiss authentic recordings, legitimate reporting or other evidence by claiming it was generated or manipulated by AI.

That said, knowing that anything can be faked tells us something about what the technology is capable of; it doesn’t tell us whether a particular piece of information is falsified. The challenge for voters is to learn how to question suspicious content without assuming everything they encounter is fake. They need practical habits that make manipulation more difficult.

First, pause when a message pushes you to act. Urgency, outrage and fear deserve extra scrutiny. Before donating, sharing or changing your voting plans, verify the request through a separate channel.

Second, look for independent confirmation. Several accounts repeating the same clip may all be relying on one unverified source. Look for credible reporting that establishes the source of the information.

Third, voters must go directly to the relevant authority. Verify registration, polling locations and deadlines with your state or local election office. For campaign communications, navigate to the campaign’s known website rather than following an unsolicited link. An official campaign statement establishes what the campaign says, while independent reporting helps assess the claim.

Finally, be comfortable saying, “I don’t know yet.” You don’t owe every viral post an immediate verdict. Waiting for evidence is a responsible decision and ensures you apply that standard even when a claim supports your political preferences.

But the responsibility extends beyond voters. These habits can help voters navigate uncertainty, but they cannot carry the full burden.

Campaigns should secure their accounts, keep original communications accessible and respond quickly to impersonation attempts. Platforms need effective reporting and escalation processes when deceptive election content appears. Nonprofit organizations such as Defending Digital Campaigns , which my organization supports as a technology partner, exist today to provide eligible campaigns with cybersecurity resources that can support this work.

AI also has an important role to play on the defensive side. The same technology that allows attackers to create convincing impersonations at greater speed and scale can help defenders identify malicious infrastructure, connect coordinated activity across channels and disrupt campaigns before they reach more people.

But technology alone will not solve the trust problem. As synthetic content becomes easier to produce, we need to make authentic information easier to verify. That means giving voters reliable places to confirm what campaigns and election officials have actually said, responding quickly when impersonation occurs.

The danger is not simply that AI will make people believe something false. It is that repeated exposure to manipulation will make them question whether anything can be trusted at all. Election security must account for both threats. Protecting the vote means protecting the systems that count it, but it also means preserving voters’ ability to know what is real.

Bobby Ford is chief strategy officer at Doppel .

articles.title: Obama prepares to rally with Michigan Dem who once delivered scathing verdict on his presidency
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed rallies with Barack Obama in Michigan, but undecided Black voters in Detroit say the endorsement hasn't swayed their decision.
articles.body: Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed is set to rally with former President Barack Obama on Saturday as Republicans raise questions about his support among Black voters, a crucial Democratic constituency in the battleground state. Obama formally endorsed the Michigan Democrat earlier this month, filming a campaign ad that ran on Oct. 12 imploring his supporters "to support Abdul El-Sayed for the United States Senate." His upcoming rally with El-Sayed has become a major political event as the progressive Senate candidate continues his effort to build bridges with the Democratic Party’s establishment. Obama's support has also renewed scrutiny of El-Sayed's past criticism of the former president, including a sharply worded 2012 essay accusing him of failing to deliver on the promises of his presidency. Conservatives have suggested that the El-Sayed campaign is leaning on Obama to build support among the African American community, whose turnout could be decisive on Election Day. ROGERS ARGUES EL-SAYED IS VULNERABLE WITH 2 TRADITIONALLY DEMOCRATIC BLOCS AS OBAMA HEADS TO MICHIGAN Claims that El-Sayed is only receiving lukewarm support from the Black community began during his primary race against Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens. El-Sayed performed strongly among Arab American voters during the Democratic primary, but he narrowly defeated Stevens after polls showed her attracting stronger support among Black Democratic voters. El-Sayed's uneven support among key Democratic constituencies has raised questions about his ability to unite the party's coalition heading into November. Black voters are crucial to the Democratic coalition in Michigan. Low turnout or defections to the GOP in Michigan among African Americans could seriously endanger the Democratic Party’s path to control of the Senate. OBAMA'S STAR POWER GETS A REALITY CHECK FROM BLACK VOTERS IN CRUCIAL SENATE RACE: 'IT'S A TURNOFF' A poll conducted by Fox News Digital in late September found that just 77% of Black voters were supportive of El-Sayed, a figure well below where Democrats typically perform with the demographic. It is unclear what impact, if any, Obama wading into Michigan’s Senate election will have. Fox News Digital spoke with more than a dozen Black voters in Detroit about Obama's endorsement, finding mixed reactions that included skepticism among undecided voters and enthusiasm from others who already planned to support El-Sayed. While the undecided voters largely agreed that Obama was still a leader within the Democratic Party, they generally did not put much weight on the former president’s endorsement of El-Sayed. "Honestly, it's a turn-off just because I've seen too many candidates use him just to manipulate the Democratic vote," Mercedes, one undecided Black voter, told Fox News Digital about Obama's endorsement. MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE ABDUL EL-SAYED SAYS LEADERS MUST ADDRESS ‘UNPAID DEBTS’ TO BLACK COMMUNITIES "What he's been able to do is from an image standpoint, as far as ‘hope,’ he drove the point there," another undecided African American voter told Fox News Digital. "But as far as really giving back to the community, minority owned businesses, and everyone across the board, I don't really think he really got there for me … he really hasn't swayed me one way or another." Rita, an undecided Black voter who said she had recently been homeless, said that Obama’s endorsement would not move the needle for her as she prefers to do her own research on candidates. Juanita, another Black voter who wasn’t sure how she would vote in November, told Fox News Digital that, "I don't want to be pushed to vote for him because somebody else is backing him." Even some African Americans who voted early for El-Sayed said Obama’s backing didn’t mean much of anything to them. SOCIALIST POLITICIANS ARE 'MORE RACIST THAN THE KKK,' SAYS BLACK DEM OFFICIAL URGING VOTERS TO DITCH EL-SAYED "I think that a lot of people put more stock into who the person is than what he does … his yay or nay doesn't sway me either way," one such voter told Fox News Digital. Undecided voters, however, had mixed feelings about El-Sayed’s changing position on Obama. "Yeah, I don't understand how you can endorse somebody that was kind of the opposition when you were in office," Juanita told Fox News Digital. "I mean, that doesn't make sense." "I think I see it as a flip flop, but I also see it as an opportunity to pretty much highlight those things and how he's actually changed and why their objectives may align now," another voter said. "You know, people's objectives change, their perspectives change." ‘DESTROYING THE AMERICAN WAY OF LIFE’: EL-SAYED’S POLITICAL ORBIT COMPLICATES EFFORT TO MODERATE HIS IMAGE Others, however, pointed out that pivots like El-Sayed’s are nothing new in politics, pointing to the fact that Vice President JD Vance was once a staunch critic of President Donald Trump. The controversy surrounding El-Sayed’s purported flip-flop on Obama can be traced back to a 2012 Huffington Post essay where he accused Obama of failing to live up to the progressive rhetoric he campaigned on. "I realize that I have little hope because there has been less change," El-Sayed wrote. "But I have to say now what I’ve been holding in throughout his campaign and what I think all of us have to admit: Obama was not the right choice — he just wasn’t the wrong one." He went on to criticize the then-president for perpetuating war, violating civil liberties and carrying out more deportations than any previous president. The Michigan Democrat has since walked back some of those criticisms, noting that it is possible to disagree with someone while still admiring them and praising how Obama operated under the circumstances he inherited. DEM INSURGENT TURNS ON THE CHARM WITH PARTY ESTABLISHMENT AS SCHUMER LEAVES BITTER FEUD HANGING Some, however, don’t buy that explanation. Conservative commentator Jason Rantz said on a CNN panel that El-Sayed was setting aside his criticisms of Obama because he was in a desperate electoral position and needed to "try to bring in black voters." Others, however, don’t think El-Sayed has a problem with Black voters at all. Kandia Milton, a government affairs professional with deep ties to Detroit's African American community, told Fox News Digital that conservative claims that El-Sayed lacks appeal to Black voters are misguided. "The great thing about Abdul is that he's not new to Detroiters. … And so Detroiters, once they understand his background, understand what he stands for and all the things that he's done in the past, you see greater enthusiasm for his campaign and his candidacy for Senate," he said. "He has been very active in getting out into the community. In fact, tomorrow we have a public meeting with Abdul at our church. Where he will be speaking to the community around, you know, the issues that he stands on and stands firm on." El-Sayed’s rally with Obama is slated to begin at 5:00 p.m. and will feature Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson and other Michigan Democrats. Attendees will be encouraged to cast early ballots in support of the Democratic ticket. articles.title: Trump joins Hannity-Earhardt wedding rehearsal dinner at Mar-a-Lago
articles.summary: Fox News hosts Sean Hannity and Ainsley Earhardt held their wedding rehearsal dinner on Friday evening at President Trump’s Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Fla. Both Trump and first lady Melania Trump were in attendance, as well as other top Trump administration officials, according to Fox News. The president is expected to attend the couple’s…
articles.body:
Fox News hosts Sean Hannity and Ainsley Earhardt held their wedding rehearsal dinner on Friday evening at President Trump’s Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Fla.

Both Trump and first lady Melania Trump were in attendance, as well as other top Trump administration officials, according to Fox News . The president is expected to attend the couple’s wedding on Saturday, which will be held at a separate location.

“I’ve had a personal relationship with President Trump for over 30 years,” Hannity said in a statement. “When Ainsley and I began planning this celebration, it was important to us that he could be part of this special time in our lives.”

Hannity added that he and Earhardt made the decision to host the dinner at Mar-a-Lago and “paid fair market value for the venue.”

“We are grateful that he and Melania could celebrate alongside our families and friends,” he continued.

The couple was dubbed the “first couple of Fox News” when they began publicly dating in 2020. They shared the news of their engagement in December 2024.

Hannity is the host of the network’s 9 p.m. show, “Hannity,” while Earhardt has co-hosted “Fox & Friends” since 2016.

Other attendees at the Friday evening celebration included Fox News colleagues, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.), Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) and U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro, among others.

In 2019, Defense Secretary and then-Fox News host Pete Hegseth married his producer at the Trump National Golf Club in Colts Neck, N.J. Trump attended the nuptials, as did Hannity, his then-colleague.

articles.title: Bill Maher to Karoline Leavitt: ‘I don’t give a s—’, ‘I like the ballroom’
articles.summary: Bill Maher, a left leaning comedian and talk show host, told former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt he actually likes President Trump’s proposed ballroom in the East Wing, despite frequent criticism from Democrats. “I don’t give a s— about any of this. I like the ballroom. America does need a ballroom,” Maher told Leavitt…
articles.body:
Bill Maher, a left leaning comedian and talk show host, told former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt he actually likes President Trump’s proposed ballroom in the East Wing, despite frequent criticism from Democrats.

“I don’t give a s— about any of this. I like the ballroom. America does need a ballroom,” Maher told Leavitt in a Friday interview on his talk show.

“It’s the United States of America,” he added. “We’re having dinner in the grass. It’s stupid.”

The pair had been discussing the report that Trump floated the idea of demolishing the press briefing room and restoring it to its prior form: a swimming pool. The president denied the report Saturday but said he could move the press briefing room “to a less obnoxious location.”

Leavitt said she did not know if Trump would actually implement the idea but that he had “been flirting with it.”

“It was a swimming pool at one time. In fact, if you go in the stairs underneath where the briefing room is, you can actually see the tile from where the pool used to be,” Leavitt said. “He just maybe wants to restore it to all of its glory. I don’t know if he’ll do it, but he’s been flirting with it.”

The 29-year-old former press secretary joined Maher’s show “Real Time” after stepping down from the role in August to spend more time with her family and young children. She has since announced plans to work for the Trump-affiliated MAGA Inc. super PAC and as a contributor on Fox News.

Maher recently attended a dinner at the White House alongside artist Kid Rock and sports commentator Stephen A. Smith, which he said during Friday’s show was an opportunity to press Trump on issues that mattered to him.

The comedian had a blunt message for those who criticized his decision to dine with Trump.

“Yeah, I did it again, b—!” Maher said. “I go and say face-to-face to the man the things you write in articles he’ll never read, but okay. You know what? F— you. I like these dinners.”

Maher told Leavitt he raised concerns about the president’s recent actions toward Ukraine at the dinner.

“The first thing I raised with the president was Starlink, and taking that down. And honestly, I think what he’s doing with Russia is unconscionable,” Maher said.

But Maher praised the president for listening to his concerns, saying, “He looks you in the eye. He never interrupts.”

“Something that I find admirable about him is he’ll look around the room and he’ll ask the opinions of everyone in it, whether it’s a low-level staffer or his chief of staff,” Leavitt replied. “He genuinely wants to know how people feel, what they think.”

Another issue Maher raised with Leavitt is how Trump may behave in the final two years of his term should Republicans perform poorly in the midterms.

Leavitt said she is not worried, telling Maher the president is always willing to work with Democrats — pointing to Trump’s cooperation with Washington Mayor Muriel Bowser.

“He has said — you’ve heard him say this — ‘I will work with Democrats to do what’s best,’” Leavitt said. “Look at what he’s done in DC with Mayor Bowser … he is always the type of guy who is willing to do that.

articles.title: Ro Khanna is wrong about the chaos in Europe — and about JD Vance
articles.summary: To paraphrase the tagline from an old horror movie, if the organized far-left anarchy that just terrified Paris and much of Europe didn’t make your skin crawl, then it’s on too tight. Protests that started in France last week saw thousands of businesses looted and burned to the ground as the anarchists danced on the…
articles.body:
To paraphrase the tagline from an old horror movie, if the organized far-left anarchy that just terrified Paris and much of Europe didn’t make your skin crawl, then it’s on too tight . Protests that started in France last week saw thousands of businesses looted and burned to the ground as the anarchists danced on the ashes.

As the shocking arson, looting and brutal violence against working-class police officers was taking place, wealthy Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) seemed to virtual signal to the anarchists and the far left here in the U.S., while taking a very calculated rhetorical shot at Vice President JD Vance.

Khanna posted on X : “From the high schools of France to the streets of Madrid to the universities of Tirana, young people are telling their governments the same thing: In an age of massive wealth inequality, they want a future they can believe in. …@JDVance says this is what happens when a nation lets in too many immigrants from the global south. He is not just morally wrong, but misreading the moment. This is what happens when nations let wealth and power accumulate in the hands of a few.”

Are they students, Congressman Khanna? Or paid anarchists and thugs?

It is quite sad (and quite telling) to see the California lawmaker lecturing Vance for “misreading the moment” while criticizing nations that “let wealth and power accumulate in the hands of a few.” Pardon me, but isn’t Khanna one of those “few” he references? Maybe he’s the one misreading things.

When he entered Congress in 2017, Khanna was the fourth richest member from California, with a reported minimum net worth of $27 million. Today, he is reported to be worth more than $340 million.

As someone who grew up in abject poverty and was homeless often as a child, I have been fighting for the rights of the poor and the disadvantaged my entire life. As such, I have never understood how looting, burning and destroying the businesses and livelihoods of store owners was a good thing. Maybe someone on the left can enlighten me.

I honestly begrudge Khanna none of his wealth or privilege in life. How truly nice it must be to marry into a millionaire family, to be placed via connections in the entitlement bubble of what Khanna describes as “the hands of a few.”

What is troubling is not the trappings of massive wealth he now enjoys, but rather his blatant hypocrisy.

Vance, of course, was not born into money. His childhood, as outlined in his bestselling memoir “Hillbilly Elegy,” deeply resonates with the working class of our nation. So why did Khanna drag him into it? Could it be that Khanna has another motivation?

Could it be that he has his eyes on the White House and is looking for some one-liners to fire at the presumptive Republican nominee that could then be inserted into his fundraising pitches to be sent out to millions?

If Khanna is truly interested in running for president, he might want to talk to a few of the tens of millions of working-class Americans in our country. They, like Vance, are not anti-immigrant. They are pro-sovereignty and pro-protected borders; they are pro-rule of law; they are pro-controlled and vetted immigration.

Those Americans understand that a nation without defined and protected borders will soon cease to be a nation. If he paid attention instead of patronized, Khanna might learn that what these Americans see happening in France and Europe at the moment petrifies them, as they fear such anarchy could soon spread like wildfire across our major cities.

If he interacted with actual working-class Americans, they would tell Khanna that France can no longer pay its bills, not only because it is a welfare state, but also because it openly allowed millions into the nation to live off an ever-shrinking government hand-out. They would further explain to some very basic economics to Khanna: Someone has to work, to pay taxes. Nothing is ever free.

These same working-class Americans would also tell Khanna that many of the anarchists in Europe who are burning and looting businesses, supposedly in protest against elites, are really just exploiting a tragic situation.

There is nothing wrong with civil protest — it is not only welcome, but often essential. And while I cannot speak for Vance, I suspect that he would relish the chance to debate Khanna on the best way to ensure the future rights of such Americans.

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.

articles.title: Stephen A Smith doubles down on Trump dinner, challenges critics by asking, 'What the f--- are you doing?'
articles.summary: Stephen A. Smith fired back at D.L. Hughley and other critics of his White House meeting with President Donald Trump, asking what they're doing for the community.
articles.body: Stephen A. Smith doubled down on defending his meeting with President Donald Trump during an episode of his "Straight Shooter" show on Thursday, challenging his critics by asking, "What the f--- are you doing?" Smith said during the show he wanted to bring several issues to Trump's attention, but his top priority was to tell the president, "With the squashing of DEI initiatives, it's essentially had a different kind of effect. It's discouraged CEOs of corporations in the private sector to be philanthropic and charitable with their money and give to HBCUs because they're fearful it will be perceived as a DEI initiative being exercised by them." "I needed the president to speak out against that, and he said he didn't think about that and that is something that he was going to tackle, not to mention the fact he followed up with a call to assure me that's exactly what he was going to tackle in a matter of days when he meets with these HBCU officials. Now I don't know what's going to happen, but I tried, as I always have and as I always will," Smith said. Have you done anything? Are you doing anything? I'm sorry for cussing. I don't mean to, apologizing to the executives at SiriusXM, but damn it. Sometimes we do stuff on the air that we do off the air. This is ridiculous. I mean, it's just, it's never enough," Smith argued. Smith repeatedly criticized comedian D.L. Hughley during the show, after Hughley questioned Smith's meeting with Trump on the "Uncertain" podcast. "I think that it says something about you when the people who hate us like you," Hughley added. "Why is it the people that hate my heroes love you?" Smith criticized Hughley over his comments, saying, "I'm sick and tired of people b----ing and moaning about what needs to be done in our community, but when somebody is actually trying to take steps to do something about it in our own small way, we selling out. We this, we that. What you doing? What you doing? It's a rhetorical question 'cause we know the answer ain't nothing but b----ing." TRUMP ADMIN'S PUSH TO SCRAP DEI IN FEDERAL GOVERNMENT TAKES LANDMARK STEP WITH NEW HIRING RULE Smith also defended his Trump meeting during an appearance on "The View" on Wednesday. He told the co-hosts he would not apologize for it. Co-host Sunny Hostin asked Smith, "He has this history of racial bias that is so clear. Did you think meeting with him, that you got anywhere?" "I don't know. We'll find out, but he’s the president of the United States, and I’ll be damned if I’m not going to try," he said. "And the reality is I’m just speaking from a constitutional perspective in that regard." He repeatedly argued that Trump would remain in office until 2028 and that people needed to deal with it. "You’re going to have to deal with him," he continued. "And when it comes to getting things done, I’m all about exhausting every means and every measure to try to do what’s in the best interest of our community. I’m not apologizing for that to anybody." Smith and Bill Maher, along with John Fetterman, are a dying breed of individuals who believe in the exchange of ideas and positions with those they all may disagree with, as exemplified by the recent dinner at the White House with President Trump and Kid Rock," Fox News contributor Joe Concha told Fox News Digital in a statement about Smith's remarks. "Unfortunately, the trend on the left is to shut down anyone through censorship or otherwise anything resembling debate."

articles.title: America’s next great addiction crisis
articles.summary: Advances in artificial intelligence and mobile technology are intensifying America’s gambling crisis by enabling predatory platforms to exploit individual psychological vulnerabilities.
articles.body:
America has a gambling problem , and it’s becoming harder to see. For decades, addiction was associated with the obvious vices: drugs, alcohol and, to a lesser extent, the desperate soul sitting at a casino table.

Today, gambling can happen anywhere, at any hour, with nothing more than a phone and a bank account. You can gamble throughout an entire football game without ever leaving the sofa. And you can lose thousands of dollars without a friend or family member even knowing.

That makes gambling addiction particularly dangerous. The addict doesn’t have to look like an addict. He can be sober and successful. He can be surrounded by people he loves while privately chasing losses on his phone. Unlike drugs or booze, gambling offers its own seductive promise of salvation. After losing a month’s salary, a gambler can convince himself that one more bet will make everything all right. Instead, one loss becomes another, and another.

Now AI threatens to make this problem many times worse. Gambling companies already collect enormous amounts of information about how customers bet, when they bet and how much they lose. AI can turn that information into a detailed picture of who is most likely to keep gambling and who is most likely to lose heavily.

The troubling question is what happens when the technology becomes better at identifying a gambler’s weaknesses than the gambler is himself.

America spent decades learning to spot a ruined life. People looked for slurred speech, bloodshot eyes, needle-marks, empty vodka bottles hidden in the laundry basket or a missing wedding ring pawned for cash.

The new system, however, leaves no real physical trace. A 25-year-old financial analyst sits in a fancy conference room in Midtown Manhattan, executing a six-figure parlay on his phone between quarterly presentations. He goes home to his apartment, eats dinner with his fiancée and then loses his entire annual bonus before the fourth quarter of a Thursday night game ends.

The brick-and-mortar casino used to force a person to cross a threshold. In 1996, if a man wanted to bet his paycheck at 3 a.m., he had to put on pants, start his car and drive somewhere specific to make a terrible decision. He had to hand paper bills to a human cashier who looked him in the eyes. That journey created natural barriers. It gave the human brain a few dozen miles to ask uncomfortable questions.

The smartphone obliterated those barriers. The casino sits in the front pocket of your jeans, right next to your mother’s text messages and dozens of work emails. It stays open at a red light, at a funeral, at a child’s piano recital, and under the covers at 2:17 a.m.

Data collection turns this total access into an asymmetric war. A gambling giant like DraftKings , which in many ways functions as a tech company, doesn’t treat its millions of users as a single, uniform crowd. Every user is an individual psychological puzzle waiting for predictive modeling to solve.

The software notes that you tend to double your wager after a heartbreaking last-second field goal. It measures the precise moment you close the app in disgust, then calculates the exact dollar amount of a “bonus bet” notification required to drag you back inside ten minutes later. This brutal system is designed to identify your impulses and monetize them, over and over again.

In many ways, it’s like nothing we have seen before. A legitimate bank deploys algorithms to flag reckless spending so the customer avoids bankruptcy and continues paying interest for 30 years. A hospital uses data to catch diseases early so the patient stays alive. A sports betting platform operates under an inverted set of incentives. The most profitable customer isn’t the cautious fan who bets $10 on the Super Bowl every February. The golden goose is the user who steadily loses, loses emotionally, and has enough liquid credit to sustain those losses over a long time.

Chemical addictions eventually demand a pause. A human body can only process a finite volume of alcohol before passing out on the carpet. A cocaine binge runs up against cardiac limits and absolute exhaustion.

Gambling works differently, because the instrument of destruction doubles as the imagined tool of salvation. When a man loses $15,000 in a night, his panicked brain doesn’t view the sportsbook app as the poison but as the only available medicine capable of producing $15,000 before sunrise. The destruction feeds the desire to do it all over again.

Traditional gambling required patience. You picked a team, placed a bet, and then waited a few hours to see who won the game. Modern micro-betting turns a contest into hundreds of tiny, high-velocity dopamine hits. You can bet on whether the next pitch in a baseball game will be a strike, whether a basketball team will make its next free throw, whether a soccer player will commit a foul before halftime, or whether a fight will break out in a hockey game within the next five minutes.

The experience feels less like sports fandom and more like a psychotic slot machine.

A recovering alcoholic doesn’t receive personalized push notifications from the local liquor store offering a free bottle of bourbon if he walks through the door before midnight. A former heroin user doesn’t open his email inbox to find a customized message offering a 20 percent discount on his next purchase because the dealer noticed he hasn’t bought anything in three weeks.

Sportsbook platforms do this continuously. With the help of AI, one should expect predation to become even more pronounced.

America has deregulated a multi-billion-dollar parasitic industry and handed it the most advanced system of psychological manipulation in human history. The consequences could be financially and socially ruinous.

John Mac Ghlionn is a writer and researcher who explores culture, society and the impact of technology on daily life.

articles.title: Bush dynasty delivers another blow to GOP in Texas Senate battle as family member breaks ranks
articles.summary: Neil Bush revealed he voted for Democrat James Talarico over Ken Paxton, citing deep concerns about Trump's influence on the Republican Party.
articles.body: Another member of the Bush family dynasty, Neil Bush, is throwing his weight behind Texas Democratic Senate hopeful James Talarico, saying he voted against a political style he believes has "damaged our country." "I have never posted a political message on Facebook, not wanting to offend friends whose views may be very different than mine. I'm breaking that tradition because I voted early today, and I voted for James Talarico for the United States Senate," Neil Bush wrote on Facebook Tuesday. "My vote was motivated by two things: deep concern about Ken Paxton's record and genuine admiration for the character and principles I see in James Talarico." BUSH FAMILY ROYALTY BACKS DEMOCRAT IN BATTLE TO FLIP TEXAS BLUE Bush, the son of former President George H.W. Bush and brother of former President George W. Bush , broke with his family's longstanding Republican political tradition in backing the Democrat. Former President George W. Bush has maintained friendly relationships with Democratic former presidents, but his relationship with President Donald Trump has been strained since the 2016 Republican presidential primary, when Trump repeatedly attacked his brother Jeb Bush and mocked their mother, former first lady Barbara Bush. "I believe Donald Trump and those who have enabled him have done enormous damage to the Republican Party. I worry about a political culture in which loyalty to an individual takes precedence over loyalty to principle, and where those who hold power begin to believe they are no longer accountable," he added. "But my vote today was about much more than opposition to Ken Paxton." Neil is the second member of the Bush family to recently throw his support behind Talarico. Barbara Bush, daughter of former President George W. Bush, contributed $2,500 on Sept. 23 to Lone Star Rising PAC, a super PAC supporting the Democrat, according to federal campaign finance records reviewed by Fox News Digital. TRUMP-LINKED MAGA INC POURS $10M INTO KEN PAXTON'S TEXAS SENATE RACE AGAINST JAMES TALARICO Lone Star Rising PAC is one of the major outside groups spending to support Talarico and oppose Paxton in the closely contested Texas Senate race, according to federal campaign finance records. The younger Bush’s support for a Democrat comes as his brother, former President George W. Bush, has increasingly embraced bipartisan relationships in his post-presidency, most recently attending the opening of former President Barack Obama’s presidential center in Chicago in June. RNC CHAIR SAYS TALARICO'S GOP CROSSOVER HOPES ARE A 'PIPE DREAM': 'NOBODY IS GOING TO FOLLOW HIM' Bush and Michelle Obama have repeatedly spoken warmly about their friendship despite their political differences. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP At the Obama Center opening, Bush even gave Michelle Obama Altoids, recreating their famous mint/cough-drop exchange from John McCain’s 2018 funeral. Fox News Digital reached out to the White House, representatives for Neil Bush and the Paxton campaign for comment.

articles.title: Donald Trump says polls are fake and insists his approval rating is really at 60%
articles.summary: A New York Times/Siena College poll put Trump’s approval at 34 percent, the lowest for a president nearing midterms since Harry Truman in 1946
articles.body:
President Donald Trump dismissed polls showing his approval rating falling ahead of November's midterm elections , insisting Americans should trust his claim that his support is closer to 60 percent.

In an interview with The Washington Examiner 's Byron York, published Saturday, Trump called the polling figures "fake" when asked about a RealClearPolitics average showing 38.8 percent of Americans approved of his job performance, while 60.4 percent disapproved.

When York pressed him on what he believed his actual approval rating was, Trump rejected the figures and insisted his support was much higher.

"The job approval, they said it's 37, 38?" Trump asked. "I'm not at 38."

Trump continued: "I don't believe I could be beaten by anybody. I think that if I needed it, which I don't, I think 60."

Trump pointed to his strong support among Republican voters and his MAGA base as evidence of his higher approval rating. However, national polling has consistently shown a less favorable picture of the president's standing.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted between October 16 and 19 found that 34 percent approved of his performance and 65 percent disapproved. A Pew Research Center survey conducted September 28 through October 4 found that just 30 percent of Americans approved of Trump's performance, while 68 percent disapproved.

A separate New York Times /Siena College poll released this week put his approval rating at 34 percent, which the newspaper said was the lowest for a president approaching midterm elections since Harry Truman's 33 percent in 1946.

Trump's rejection of polling figures comes amid a controversy involving The New York Times and Wedgewood Research, a polling firm that acknowledged producing fabricated polling numbers as part of a social experiment. The newspaper said it did not use the disputed polls when calculating Trump's job approval rating.

To support his claim that he remains popular, Trump pointed to an analysis by CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten showing the president's support among MAGA Republicans remains near 100 percent. Enten reported that Trump received 99 percent of the MAGA Republican vote in the 2024 election and had a 98 percent approval rating among MAGA Republicans in September.

"I think I'd be in the 60s now. Now, in the Republican Party, I'm way up. Show him the 99 percent. Have you seen it?" Trump said.

However, Enten also found that Trump's net approval rating on inflation fell from +8 points in 2024 to -45 ahead of the midterms .

This week, Enten called the president's polling situation "a five-alarm Trumpster fire" after a Reuters/Ipsos survey put Trump's approval rating at 31 percent, the lowest recorded for him across both of his presidential terms.

Despite the unfavorable figures, Trump continued praising Enten and CNN for polling that reflects his support among Republican voters.

"They did do some nice polls on me, I must say. If CNN keeps doing those polls, I'll like them more and more," Trump said.

articles.title: Trump says he may move White House press corps to new location
articles.summary: Trump’s remarks come amid a fractious moment between the US president and the journalists who cover him.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has confirmed he could move the White House press corps to a different location, possibly away from the executive residence.

In a social media post on Friday, Trump described reports that he planned to remove the White House press briefing room in favour of restoring a historic swimming pool located underneath as “Fake News”.

“I NEVER even thought to do such a stupid thing!” he wrote in a Truth Social post.

Trump, however, indicated he may relocate dozens of reporters who cover the White House “to a less obnoxious location”.

The New York Times on Tuesday reported that Trump had pitched his former press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, on an idea to move journalists out of the White House’s storied James S. Brady Press Briefing Room. That proposal did not move forward during Leavitt’s tenure, which ended on August 27.

Trump’s remarks come amid a fractious moment between him and the journalists who cover him.

Last month, Trump banned journalists from three US-based media outlets – CNN, MS NOW and POLITICO – from the White House, a move that proponents of free speech said violated First Amendment protections.

A US federal judge ruled that the order was likely unconstitutional, forcing the White House to restore the journalists’ access. The Trump administration continues to fight the ruling.

Trump has also regularly chided and denigrated members of the media he claims cover him unfairly.

The latest incident was during an Oval Office event on Tuesday when Trump attacked The Independent’s White House Correspondent Andrew Feinberg.

“What’s wrong with you? Are you a sick person? I actually think there’s something wrong with you”, Trump said as Feinberg tried to ask a question. The moment was amplified by the White House on social media.

If Trump opts to proceed with changes to the White House press briefing room, it would be the latest in a long list of controversial projects he has ordered that would transform the property.

Since returning to power last year, the US president has demolished the White House East Wing to construct a new ballroom, installed concrete pavers over the lawn centred in the White House Rose Garden and built a helipad on the South Lawn.

The Times reported Trump told aides he wanted to bring back a West Wing indoor pool constructed in 1933 for use by President Franklin D Roosevelt, who suffered from polio and often swam, according to his presidential library, to ease soreness.

In the 1970s, former President Richard Nixon had a floor constructed above the pool to accommodate a briefing room for the growing White House press corps. The pool remains beneath the floor of the briefing room.

Leavitt confirmed during a Friday interview that Trump was “flirting” with the idea of restoring the pool.

“He just, maybe, wants to restore it to all of its glory”, Leavitt said during an appearance on HBO’s “Real Time with Bill Maher”. “I don’t know if he’ll do it.”

The White House did not immediately return Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

articles.title: El-Sayed spats with Baier over Muslim Brotherhood question: ‘Be a journalist’
articles.summary: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed pushed back at Fox News’s Bret Baier in an interview that aired on Friday evening over questions about his alleged ties to an Islamist political group. After Baier began asking the candidate about accusations repeatedly made by his opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), that the Democrat has ties…
articles.body:
Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed pushed back at Fox News’s Bret Baier in an interview that aired on Friday evening over questions about his alleged ties to an Islamist political group.

After Baier began asking the candidate about accusations repeatedly made by his opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), that the Democrat has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, El-Sayed cut him off.

“Let me just stop you right there,” the Democrat said. “You are asking this question to raise a question about whether or not I have dual loyalty.”

The journalist replied, “I’m not,” and returned to reading the campaign’s accusations.

El-Sayed interrupted him again and accused Baier of trying to take things “out of context” and asked him to “be a journalist.”

“As a journalist, if you’re asking about my allegiance to the constitution, I have never been a member of the Muslim Brotherhood, I never will be a member of the Muslim Brotherhood,” El-Sayed said.

“I’m interested in serving the United States,” he continued. “I’m interested in swearing an oath to the constitution that every senator has sworn an oath to.”

In an appearance on Fox News’s “Special Report with Bret Baier” after the interview with El-Sayed aired, Rogers repeated his claim that El-Sayed “has adopted the ideology of the Muslim Brotherhood.”

El-Sayed would be the first Muslim senator if he wins Michigan’s open Senate race. He has faced numerous attacks on the campaign trail about his family background and faith, including past comments made by his mother and half-sister.

Rogers and other Republicans have pointed to a 2012 open letter signed on to by the Michigan Democrat to then newly elected Egyptian president, Mohamed Morsi, whose political party represented the Muslim Brotherhood’s political wing.

The letter’s signatories urged Morsi “to purge the media and police as quickly as possible.”

El-Sayed’s campaign has repeatedly denied that the Democrat has any connection to the Muslim Brotherhood, and he has publicly disavowed the group.

President Trump notably designated Lebanese, Jordanian and Egyptian chapters of the Muslim Brotherhood as terrorist organizations in the U.S.
